title: The Spirit of truth (John 16:12–15)
hook: I have many things to say but you cannot bear them now

segments.voice: Yesterday, I have called you friends: the ones who are told everything. Your line was friends, not servants. Who did you tell the why to? Day five hundred twenty-three.

A good doctor doesn't read you the whole chart in the first five minutes. A good parent doesn't explain everything about death to a four-year-old at bedtime. A good teacher doesn't start calculus on the first day of algebra. Not because they're hiding something, but because there's an order to understanding. Some things you can only carry when you're ready. Yesterday Jesus said he'd told his friends everything he heard from the Father. Today, still at the table, he says something that sounds like the opposite.
screen: `NOT THE WHOLE CHART AT ONCE.` → `AN ORDER TO UNDERSTANDING.` → `IT SOUNDS LIKE THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth." So which is it? Has he told them everything, or not? Both, in a way. Everything has been given in him. But they can't carry it all yet. Bear is a carrying word, the kind you'd use for a heavy load. It's honest about the disciples. These are men who, within hours, will fall asleep in the garden and run. They're not ready for the whole of it, and Jesus doesn't pretend they are. So he promises the Spirit of truth, who will teach them, or in the Greek, guide them, lead them along the way, into all the truth. Not dump it on them. Walk them into it. And the Spirit, Jesus says, won't bring a new message of his own. He'll take what is mine and show it to you. Catholics hear in this promise the Church's long, slow understanding of what it received. The Second Vatican Council taught that the understanding of what has been handed down grows over time, through contemplation, study and the experience of believers. In the nineteenth century John Henry Newman, now a canonized saint, wrote a whole book on how doctrine develops, the way a living thing grows up without turning into something else. Not new revelation, the Church says, but deeper understanding of what was given. Not yet, but coming.
screen: `YOU CANNOT BEAR THEM NOW.` · `HE WILL GUIDE YOU INTO ALL TRUTH.` · `NOT NEW: WHAT IS MINE, SHOWN.` · `NEWMAN: DOCTRINE GROWS LIKE A LIFE.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT OF TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a question wait. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you don't understand yet, about your faith, your life, a person, a loss. Don't try to solve it. Imagine setting it on a table in front of you, not thrown away, just set down to come back to later. Notice whether your shoulders loosen a little. If you pray, you can hold Jesus's promise, he will teach you all truth, and leave the question with him. If you don't, simply let it rest on the table. The bell holds the time.
The Spirit of truth. Jesus's promise that the Spirit will guide his friends into the truth they can't yet carry. Today's word.
Your line: not yet, but coming. Today, when you hit something you don't understand, say not yet, instead of never. Day five hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics pray to the Holy Spirit for understanding, especially at Pentecost and before study or decisions, often with the traditional prayer "Come, Holy Spirit."

fork.setup: you're Jesus at the supper. your friends are exhausted and frightened, and there's much more they need to know. what do you do?
options: tell them all of it now, while there's time.
tell them they can't bear it now, and promise the Spirit.
fork.reveal: I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now. the Spirit of truth will lead them into it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus left some things out.
what it means: he gave everything, but promised the Spirit to lead them into it at a pace they could bear.
what a scholar hears: hodēgēsei means will guide, lead the way; Vatican II's Dei Verbum 8 speaks of growth in understanding of tradition; Newman's Essay on Development appeared in 1845.

sources.quoted: I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): light polish only ('bear' line reworded so it doesn't read as a word-origin claim).
Hodēgeō as 'guide, lead the way' (KJV 'guide you into all truth'; Douay 'teach you all truth' following the Vulgate 'docebit'). Confirm.
Dei Verbum 8 on growth in understanding through contemplation, study and experience: paraphrased. Confirm.
Newman: growth compared to a living thing that stays itself; paraphrase of the Essay's argument. Confirm.
